title: The Lighthouse That Answered from Land
cues: At two in the morning, the island's lighthouse got an answer. Three short flashes. Three long. Three short. A distress signal. The odd part? It came from half a mile inland.
Bea had kept the light for eleven winters. She knew where every boat ought to be. She also knew the hill behind the lighthouse had been a sheep field since before she was born.
She checked the sea first. Nothing but fog and the light sweeping across it. Then she covered the cabin lamp with her coat and uncovered it twice. Two flashes came back from the hill.
She called the harbour. The dispatcher asked for a vessel name. Bea looked at the pasture. Put down sheep, she said. She grabbed a torch and headed for the old road.

Halfway up the hill the flashes vanished. Three steps back, they appeared again. Whoever was signalling could see the lighthouse balcony perfectly. They couldn't see a person standing ten feet to the left.
At the top stood a bus shelter. On its roof, a square of glass caught Bea's torch and threw it straight into her eyes. She stepped sideways. The whole hill went dark again.
It was a mirror. Years ago, a farmer had put it there to see traffic coming round the bend. Bea followed the angle with her torch. It pointed down toward the abandoned quarry.
The quarry had filled with rain. At the bottom, balanced on the roof of a stalled van, was the island postman. The only light he could see was the beam reflected in that old mirror.
His phone was soaked. His torch had one bar left. Every time the lighthouse swept past the shelter, he'd aimed for the square that lit up. He'd been doing it for nearly an hour.
Bea radioed the quarry entrance. This time she had a useful address. The rescue crew brought the postman up the access ramp in a little boat. He kept one arm wrapped around a blue bag.
She expected an urgent parcel. Maybe medicine. He opened it on the bank. Inside was his lunch and a perfectly dry phone charger. They laughed so hard the dispatcher asked if everybody was all right.
The next morning the harbour report needed a name for the vessel involved. Bea looked at the little rescue boat, then at the sheep by the shelter. She left the first entry exactly as it was.
